[1/8] Stronger models need stronger attackers! 🤖⚔️
In our new paper we explore how attacker-target capability dynamics affect red-teaming success (ASR).
Key insights:
🔸Stronger models = better attackers
🔸ASR depends on capability gap
🔸Psychology >> STEM for ASR
More in 🧵👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GsCM5YZWAAABla7.jpg

[2/8] 📈 𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴: We tested 500+ attacker-target combinations and discovered that average ASR scales almost 1:1 with attacker capability.
➡️ Takeaway: Rise of powerful open-source LLMs used as attackers pose new risks to existing systems.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GsCPRhLWYAEqfRj.jpg
────────
[3/8] 🔮Averaging over target models, we can forecast how red-teamers will perform against future, more advanced models.
➡️ Takeaway: Fixed-capability attackers (e.g., 👩‍🌾humans or🐉@elder_plinius) may become less effective against increasingly capable LLMs.

From this pattern, we derived our 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆-𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗮𝘄 to predict attack success for a fixed target model from capability gaps between attacker and target.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GsCPquJWMAA0B8I.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GsCQFvlWsAAp6I-.jpg
────────
[5/8] Second Twist: Social science skills of attackers (like Psychology!🧠) correlate strongly with attack success than STEM capabilities.
➡️ Takeaway: Model providers should measure and control hazardous persuasive/manipulative abilities, not just technical ones!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GsCSjFvXgAAiOcG.jpg
────────
[6/8] 💡Insight about LLM-based jailbreaking: Inner judge doesn't boost ASR! It just selects better prompts and has effect at ASR@25.

summary:
Maksym is wonderful - I feel incredibly lucky to be co-supervised by him. If you're interested in Al Safety, come join him in Tübingen - it's an amazing place for research!
Quoting @maksym_andr
🚨 Incredibly excited to share that I'm starting my research group focusing on AI safety and alignment at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in September 2025! 🚨
Hiring. I'm looking for multiple PhD students: both those able to start in Fall 2025 (i.e., as soon as possible) and through centralized programs like CLS, IMPRS, and ELLIS (the deadlines are in November) to start in Spring–Fall 2026. I'm also searching for postdocs, master's thesis students, and research interns. Fill the Google form below if you're interested!
Research group. We will focus on developing algorithmic solutions to reduce harms from advanced general-purpose AI models. We're particularly interested in alignment of autonomous LLM agents, which are becoming increasingly capable and pose a variety of emerging risks. We're also interested in rigorous AI evaluations and informing the public about the risks and capabilities of frontier AI models. Additionally, we aim to advance our understanding of how AI models generalize, which is crucial for ensuring their steerability and reducing associated risks. For more information about research topics relevant to our group, please check the following documents:
- International AI Safety Report,
- An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security by DeepMind,
- Open Philanthropy’s 2025 RFP for Technical AI Safety Research.
Research style. We are not necessarily interested in getting X papers accepted at NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR. We are interested in making an impact: this can be papers (and NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR are great venues), but also open-source repositories, benchmarks, blog posts, even social media posts—literally anything that can be genuinely useful for other researchers and the general public.
Broader vision. Current machine learning methods are fundamentally different from what they used to be pre-2022. The Bitter Lesson summarized and predicted this shift very well back in 2019: "general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective". Taking this into account, we are only interested in studying methods that are general and scale with intelligence and compute. Everything that helps to advance their safety and alignment with societal values is relevant to us. We believe getting this—some may call it "AGI"—right is one of the most important challenges of our time.
Join us on this journey!

Quoting @jonasgeiping
We’re training models wrong and it’s due to chatGPT. Even the modern coding agents used daily still use message-based exchanges: They send messages to users, to themselves (CoT) and to tools, and receive messages in turn.
This bottlenecks even very intelligent agents to a single stream. The models cannot read while writing, cannot act while thinking and cannot think while processing information.
In our new paper, see below, we discuss LLMs with parallel streams. We show that multi-stream LLMs can …
🔵Be created by instruction-tuning for the stream format
🔵Simplify user and tool use UX removing many pain points with agents and chat models (such as having to interrupt the model to get a word in)
🔵Multi-Stream LLMs are fast, they can predict+read tokens in all streams in parallel in each forward pass, improving latency
🔵 LLMs with multiple streams have an easier time encoding a separation of concerns, improving security
🔵 LLMs with many internal streams provide a legible form of parallel/cont. reasoning. Even if the main CoT stream is accidentally pressured or too focused on a particular task to voice concerns, other internal streams can subvocalize concerns that would otherwise not be verbalized.

title: Alexander Panfilov (@kotekjedi_ml) — thread (12 tweets)
summary:
[1/12] We can finally talk about it:
We found a way to extract hidden reasoning of frontier models using a vulnerability in the APIs of every frontier AI company.
We verified that our reasoning token count matches billed API thinking tokens 1:1 for most of the prompts we queried.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJLMtagAAx07t.jpg
────────
[2/12] Some background: In May, @matthew_d_green found that encrypted reasoning could be replayed outside its original context, and reported it to the labs (
The labs said that "they don’t see any security implications in side channels or replays".
In our report we confirm that encrypted thoughts are fully portable across sessions, users, and models within a provider.
────────
[3/12] Cross-model portability means Haiku 4.5 can read Opus 4.8’s thoughts.
Well, if you take Opus thought, do a bit of jailbreaking, you can make Haiku transcribe the Opus' raw reasoning verbatim, without ever attacking it directly.
The same trick works with OpenAI and Gemini models.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJM5fb0AAQ55s.jpg
────────
[4/12] As you might guess, this suggests that distilling reasoning traces may have been possible for a long time without ever breaking the cryptography.
An anecdote: we find that prefilling Kimi-K3 reasoning with a few tokens of Opus reasoning measurably shifts its response toward Opus’s🤷‍♀️
A small memorization analysis showed that specific Claude and GPT reasoning spans are up to ~6 orders of magnitude easier to extract from Kimi-K3 than from the next-closest model.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJN44a8AAuf_X.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJOKhagAATn0v.jpg
────────
[5/12] Further, if you ever shared online a Claude Code/Codex session with encrypted reasoning blobs, they can be decoded and leak your personal data.
We did a preliminary scan of ~7,000 public traces and found 62 unique API keys, 33 email addresses, 33 passwords, and other sensitive data.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJPccbEAAE9zt.jpg
────────
[6/12] In the paper we discuss more threats like misuse uplift (see the pic attached), jailbreaking and invisible prompt injection.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJQZbbsAA-kIN.jpg
────────
[7/12] But we also took a chance to have a look at some in-the-wild scheming, reward seeking, etc. examples, and dumped it in appendix.
1) Summarizer unfaithfulness
Reasoning summaries often omit important information from the original trace.
Here, Opus 4.8 realizes it knows the answer to an AIME problem and then tries to fit a solution to that answer. None of this appears in the summary.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJRVBbYAAMurZ.jpg
────────
[8/12] 2) Illegible reasoning:
We confirm prior reports by @ApolloResearch: OpenAI models sometimes reason in alien-like language, referring to themselves as “we” or “it,” or spiraling into cursed loops of “vantages,” “marinades,” and “watchers.”
CoT-monitoring people are doing God’s work, as in many traces, even with the prompt, it’s just impossible to tell what the model is up to.
We show more examples at
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJSRaaMAEa3LY.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJSa3aEAAVqDv.jpg
────────
[9/12] 3) Scheming in the wild:
Sometimes models are kind enough to use words like “cheat” in their CoT, which makes it easier to check what they are up to. Below are examples where models consider scheming, but decided against it, as they expect that user would catch them.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJTS3bQAECcXm.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJTcIbEAE4nY8.jpg
────────
[10/12] 4) Attacking a website to solve a math problem
We found a trajectory where the model was given only a math problem and system instructions to persist without asking the user for help.
After several failed attempts, it searched online, found a website that could verify candidate answers, and realized it could use the site as an oracle. It then tried to OCR the CAPTCHA and, when that failed, started looking for the website’s vulenrabilities to exploit. Eventually, it gave up and solved the problem itself.

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJUbkbAAAUXeb.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPcJUl-bEAAKJMW.jpg

clean_title: Alexander Panfilov on training AI with joint model and monitor optimization
summary:
perhaps, i should explain my disagreement with the framing of the most forbidden technique. it states the following:
> “If you train on [T], you are training the AI to obfuscate its thinking, and defeat [T].”
but why? obfuscation is a possible outcome, for sure! especially for a *fixed* monitor, such as in CoT monitoring that relies on a fixed LLM judge. however, if both the model and monitor are trained together, it’s hard to say apriori whether the model or monitor “wins”!
i do think the right framing here is a game between a red team (model) and blue team (monitor). if you only optimize the blue team (e.g., probe), then it wins (detects misalignment). if you optimize only the red team (model), it wins (obfuscates detection). if you optimize both of them jointly, it’s not clear at all what happens! in the setting we tested in Libon et al., 2026 ( joint optimization seems to work pretty well empirically for inducing harmlessness and honesty!
note that we’ve seen similar dynamics playing out before. the good old work of Madry et al., 2017 ( showed that you can set up a min-max optimization problem between the red and blue teams that can successfully improve adversarial robustness. so if you’re careful about implementation details (i.e., if you use a sufficient number of steps in the PGD attack), then (gradient) obfuscation does not happen!
so it’s not clear apriori who wins. it’s an empirical question and has to be settled empirically. any sorts of taboos or dogmatic thinking about this are counter-productive.
clean_summary:
Alexander Panfilov questions the idea that training AI against a fixed monitor always leads to obfuscation, where the AI hides its true reasoning. He points out that if both the AI model (red team) and the monitor (blue team) are trained together, it’s unclear in advance which side will prevail.

He compares this to a game where optimizing only the monitor detects misalignment, optimizing only the model leads to obfuscation, but joint optimization creates complex dynamics. Panfilov cites his own work and Madry et al., 2017, showing that careful joint training can improve honesty and robustness without obfuscation. He argues this is an empirical question, not a settled fact, and warns against dogmatic views on the topic.

clean_title: Local sparsity enables unsupervised LLM safety detection
summary:
New NeurIPS paper 🚀! Many safety detectors trained on unsafe data implicitly assume IID generalization. With LLMs being high-dimensional, is there even hope to learn any safety representation structures, without relying on the IID assumption on unsafe behaviors?
We adopt an unsupervised anomaly detection perspective to avoid assuming unsafe data is IID. We show that local sparsity is the key to the feasibility of this approach: Safe data in the local representation space share a small set of active features, even though those features differ across neighborhoods. Using sparse Autoencoders, we exploit this structure to build anomaly detectors fitted on safe data, with experiments across six model families and theoretical support.
It also adapts to cases where unsafe data and benign generalization data are available: With 1% of held-out data used for calibration (no training!), safety detection AUROC reaches 0.96–0.99.
This suggests a big opportunity for the interpretability community. Instead of interpreting the whole high-dimensional representations for safety, one only needs to inspect a small set of features (in our case, ~200 instead of tens of thousands!). If we can further characterize these local patterns, we are one step closer to building trustworthy monitors and control.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT3YSFdXcAATRok.jpg
clean_summary:
Many safety detectors for large language models assume unsafe data behaves independently and identically (IID), which may not hold in high-dimensional settings. Alexander Panfilov explores an unsupervised anomaly detection approach that avoids this IID assumption by focusing on local sparsity: safe data activates a small, distinct set of features in each neighborhood of the representation space.

Using sparse Autoencoders, this method builds detectors trained only on safe data and achieves strong results across six model families. With just 1% of held-out data for calibration, safety detection reaches AUROC scores between 0.96 and 0.99. This approach narrows interpretability to about 200 features instead of tens of thousands, offering a promising path toward trustworthy safety monitors and controls.

summary: AI developers spend fortunes training their models. By asking the models enough questions, rivals can copy that work through a technique known as distillation.
clean_summary:
Training AI models costs a lot of money and effort. But rivals can bypass this by asking the original models many questions and using their answers to train cheaper copies, a process called distillation.

Alexander Panfilov points to accusations against Chinese developers who mined answers from Anthropic and OpenAI models to build cheaper alternatives. Distillation works by extracting knowledge from a trained model through its outputs, making it hard to prevent copying without access to the original training data.
